Optimal Contention Resolution from Samples

Shaddin Dughmi ††thanks: Department of Computer Science, University of Southern California. shaddin@usc.edu. Supported by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research under award number FA9550-24-1-0261. Part of this work was done while the author was on sabbatical as the Carter and Tania Neild visiting professor at Northwestern University, as well as a visiting professor in the Data Science Institute at the University of Chicago.    Vasilis Livanos ††thanks: Department of Computer Science, University of Southern California. vas.livanos@gmail.com. Supported by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research under award number FA9550-24-1-0261.    Pranav Nuti ††thanks: Booth School of Business, University of Chicago. pranav.nuti@chicagobooth.edu.
Abstract

Contention resolution schemes (CRSs) convert random sets which are ex-ante feasible for some constraint into sets which are feasible ex post, and their online variants (ROCRSs and OCRSs) have broad applications in Bayesian and stochastic optimization, including prophet inequalities and stochastic probing. In many such applications, however, full distributional knowledge is an unattainable requirement. This motivates the study of contention resolution schemes which employ a limited number of samples from the underlying distributions.

In this paper, we study sample-based contention resolution for kk-uniform matroids, for both uniformly random and adversarial arrival orders, and compare their balance guarantees to the best possible with full distributional knowledge. For a single-item constraint, we show that one sample per element suffices for an optimal (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-balanced ROCRS. For adversarial arrivals, however, we prove that no single-sample OCRS can be 1/21/2-balanced, even for known arrival orders, separating contention resolution from prophet inequalities in the single-sample setting. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that two samples are necessary and sufficient for the optimal 1/21/2 guarantee. We also complement our results with a single-sample 0.480.48-balanced scheme.

For general kk, we give a simple single-sample ROCRS that achieves an optimal balance ratio of 1−e−k​kk/k!1-e^{-k}k^{k}/k!. In adversarial order, we obtain a single-sample (1−O⁡(1/k))\left(1-\operatorname{O}(1/\sqrt{k})\right)-balanced scheme, matching the optimal asymptotic dependence on kk.

Finally, we complete the picture by characterizing the minimum number of samples needed to match the optimal balance ratio achievable with full distributional knowledge. For random arrivals, one sample suffices for k∈{1,2,3,4}k\in\left\{1,2,3,4\right\}, and zero samples suffice for k≥5k\geq 5. For an adversarial arrival order, even known in advance, and any k≥2k\geq 2, we show that no constant number of samples suffices for achieving optimal balance.

Keywords: contention resolution; decision making under uncertainty; online algorithms; rounding algorithms.

1 Introduction

Contention resolution has emerged as a fundamental algorithmic primitive, abstracting the familiar task of turning a random set which satisfies a system of constraints ex-ante, i.e., on average, into one which satisfies them ex-post, i.e., always. Originally formulated as a tool for enforcing feasibility in randomized rounding of linear programs Chekuri et al. (2014), it has since found many more applications to online and stochastic decision making problems such as prophet inequalities, stochastic probing, secretary problems, and more (e.g. Feldman et al. (2021); Adamczyk and Włodarczyk (2018); Lee and Singla (2018); Dughmi (2025); Bechtel and Dughmi (2021); Dughmi et al. (2023)). The broad reach of contention resolution arguably stems from the fact that it provides per-element guarantees: a cc-balanced contention resolution scheme (CRS) selects an element ii with probability at least cc when ii is active, meaning it is available for selection. This lends itself to objective-agnostic guarantees that hold across problems: all linear objectives, and many more, are preserved up to the same cc factor.

Despite the aforementioned generality, the literature on contention resolution relies on a strong assumption: the distribution of active elements—which is described fully by the marginal activation probabilities pip_{i} for product distributions—is known and given up front. Indeed, activation probabilities feature prominently in the design of optimal contention resolution schemes, even for the simplest of constraint systems. This precludes applying contention resolution to settings where the distribution may be difficult to describe exactly, or must be learned from (perhaps limited) historical data. Somewhat surprisingly, much remains open with regards to optimal contention resolution from samples, even for product distributions and the simplest of constraints, despite the fact that the analogous question has been studied extensively for the closely-related setting of prophet inequalities Azar et al. (2014); Rubinstein et al. (2020); Fu et al. (2024); Cristi and Ziliotto (2024); Ezra (2026).

In this paper, we study contention resolution from samples for the simplest of settings: product distributions with unknown activation probabilities pip_{i} for each element ii, for kk-uniform matroid constraints (also known as cardinality constraints), paying special attention to the single-item (k=1k=1) setting. We consider online arrivals in adversarial or random order and ask the following question:

How many samples are needed, per element, to obtain an optimal online contention resolution scheme?

1.1 Results and Techniques

We consider online contention resolution in both the adversarial and random order settings, for single-item and kk-uniform matroid constraints. For the precise problem statement and relevant definitions, see Section 2.

Single-item.

For the simplest case of a single-item constraint with known activation probabilities, there is a (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-balanced Random Order Contention Resolution Scheme (ROCRS) Adamczyk and Włodarczyk (2018) and a 1/21/2-balanced Online Contention Resolution Scheme (OCRS) when the elements arrive in adversarial order Feldman et al. (2021). Both guarantees are the best possible in their respective settings, and in fact the 1−1/e1-1/e guarantee is optimal even for offline contention resolution.

We show a dichotomy between the random and adversarial order settings: we design a (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-balanced single-item ROCRS that uses a single sample per element, whereas we show that every single-sample single-item OCRS has its balance ratio bounded away from the optimal ratio of 1/21/2. Our ROCRS is quite simple: active elements are accepted greedily, except that each element whose sample is also active is discarded with probability 1/e1/e. Our impossibility result for adversarial arrivals is through a case analysis on a small example.

Though a single sample does not suffice for an optimal OCRS, we show, perhaps surprisingly, that two samples do suffice. Our two-sample 1/21/2-balanced OCRS is based on the following simple yet powerful observation: a scheme which chooses a start time TT such that Pr[T=0]=1/2\Pr[T=0]=1/2 and Pr[T=i]=pi/2\Pr[T=i]=p_{i}/2 for all ii, and accepts the first active element arriving strictly after TT, is 1/21/2-balanced. We show how to sample such a TT using only the two samples per element. This is closely related to the Bernoulli race problem studied in Dughmi et al. (2021), and more broadly to the literature on combinatorial Bernoulli factories Niazadeh et al. (2021); Niazadeh et al. (2023); Niazadeh et al. (2024), though we are not aware of any constant sample factories for such problems.11 1 The connection between our problem and that of the two-sample Bernoulli race runs quite deep, with reductions in both directions. We defer the interesting details to the full version of this paper, or perhaps a future paper! Our approach to sampling TT is different and interesting in its own right, however: we reduce sampling TT to none other than a different contention resolution problem, this time offline and with a single sample! In particular, by using one set of samples to design a 1/21/2-balanced CRS for the other, and enforcing the balance guarantee with equality, we obtain the desired pi/2p_{i}/2 probabilities. We lean on a CRS of Feige and Vondrák Feige and Vondrák (2010), modifying it appropriately to use a single sample and enforce the balance of 1/21/2 with equality, to accomplish just that.

Finally, we show that a single sample per element can be used to approximate this distribution of TT and obtain a 0.480.48-balanced OCRS. While this result is not tight, our aforementioned impossibility provides an upper bound strictly smaller than 1/21/2.

General kk.

We next turn our attention to general kk-uniform matroid constraints. When activation probabilities are known, these admit an optimal (1−e−k​kk/k!)(1-e^{-k}k^{k}/k!)-balanced ROCRS Arnosti and Ma (2021) which is optimal even for the offline setting of contention resolution Chekuri et al. (2014); Yan (2011). When the elements arrive in adversarial order, no general closed-form expression in kk is known for the optimal balance ratio, but it is implicitly characterized by a factor-revealing linear program Jiang et al. (2023).

For random arrivals, we show that a single sample per element again suffices to recover the optimal (1−e−k​kk/k!)(1-e^{-k}k^{k}/k!) guarantee for every kk. Our ROCRS accepts the first kk active elements, except that the kk-th is discarded with probability k/(2​k+1)k/(2k+1) if its sample is also active; if discarded, it is replaced by the next active element. In other words, our ROCRS greedily selects the first k−1k-1 active elements without looking at their samples, and only uses the sample of the kk-th active element to decide between that or the (k+1)(k+1)-th active element. We also give an alternative proof in Appendix B, using a different scheme that directly generalizes our single-item ROCRS.

For adversarial arrivals, we design a single-sample (1−O⁡(1/k))\left({1-O\left({1/\sqrt{k}}\right)}\right)-balanced OCRS, matching the asymptotically optimal dependence on kk Alaei (2014); Jiang et al. (2023). Our approach is a single-sample analogue of the OCRS of Dinev and Weinberg Dinev and Weinberg (2024): we use the samples in place of the known activation probabilities to control how quickly we accept elements. More specifically, we admit an active element as a candidate if the resulting number of candidates does not exceed the number of active samples among the elements that have arrived, plus a random allowance of order k\sqrt{k}. We then select among the candidates online, giving each the same acceptance probability while ensuring that we accept at most kk elements.

Sample complexity.

Finally, we investigate the exact sample complexity of optimal schemes, in particular as we vary kk. We find a surprising contrast between random and adversarial arrivals: increasing kk reduces the required number of samples per element in the case of random arrivals, but does the reverse for adversarial arrivals.

For random order arrivals, we determine the minimum number of samples per element needed to achieve the optimal balance ratio: one for k∈{1,2,3,4}k\in\left\{1,2,3,4\right\}, and zero for k≥5k\geq 5. The latter follows directly from a result of Arnosti and Ma (Arnosti and Ma, 2021, Lemma 6), as greedily accepting the first kk active elements already yields the optimal guarantee when k≥5k\geq 5. For k≤4k\leq 4, we show that no scheme using zero samples can be better than k/(k+1)k/(k+1)-balanced, strictly below the optimum. This impossibility also holds for offline contention resolution, and therefore so does the characterization.

For adversarial arrivals, we show a striking separation between the single-item case and larger cardinality constraints, where the latter require more samples (reversing the trend observed for random arrivals). Whereas two samples per element suffice to recover the optimal guarantee for known activation probabilities when k=1k=1, no constant number of samples suffices for any k≥2k\geq 2! This impossibility holds even when the arrival order is known in advance, and even if the number of samples is allowed to depend on kk. Our proof builds on the characterization of Jiang, Ma, and Zhang Jiang et al. (2023): we construct two families of instances for which optimality requires the probability of accepting at least two elements in an initial segment to tend to zero in one family and stay bounded away from zero in the other. We then show that a fixed number of samples cannot support this difference.

1.2 Additional Discussion of Related Work

There is a large literature on contention resolution and closely-related stochastic decision problems, most notably prophet inequalities, with known prior distributions. We cannot hope to do justice to this vast literature, and instead refer the reader to related work discussions in Dughmi (2025) and Aminian et al. (2026). Below, we overview work on contention resolution and related problems from samples, as that is most relevant to our focus in this paper.

Contention Resolution.

To our knowledge, there are few papers discussing contention resolution from samples. The work of Fu, Lu, Tang, Turkieltaub, Wu, Wu and Zhang Fu et al. (2022) considers oblivious schemes that have neither distributional knowledge nor access to any samples. They design a 1/e1/e-balanced oblivious OCRS for the single-item case with adversarial arrivals, and show that this is the best possible without distributional information, implying a separation from the setting with known activation probabilities. The same work also considers schemes with sample access, and shows that certain matroid constraints prohibit constant balance guarantees with constantly-many samples per element. Subsequent work by Fu, Lu, Tang, Wu, Wu and Zhang Fu et al. (2024) designed a (1/4−ε)(1/4-\varepsilon)-balanced OCRS for matroid constraints with Oε⁡((log⁡n)4)\operatorname{O}_{\varepsilon}(\left({\log{n}}\right)^{4}) samples per element, for any ε>0\varepsilon>0. Recently, Feldman, Svensson and Zenklusen Feldman et al. (2026) improved upon this by achieving the same balance guarantee using only O⁡(log⁡r​(log⁡log⁡r)2)O\left({\log{r}(\log{\log{r}})^{2}}\right) many samples, almost matching the Ω⁡(log⁡r)\operatorname{\Omega}\left({\log{r}}\right) lower bound due to Fu et al. (2024), where rr is the rank of the matroid.

Prophet Inequalities and Related Problems.

Closely related to online contention resolution are prophet inequality problems. Here, elements arrive online in adversarial order, and instead of per-element activations we get per-element rewards viv_{i}. The goal is to achieve a high total reward, competing with an omniscient prophet. In contrast to contention resolution, there has been a large body of work studying prophet inequalities from samples. A single sample suffices for an optimal factor of 1/21/2 in the single-choice setting Rubinstein et al. (2020); Correa et al. (2026), as well as for an asymptotically-optimal guarantee in the kk-choice setting as kk grows large Azar et al. (2019). The same question has also been studied for more elaborate constraints, as well as random order arrivals (known as prophet secretary problems). Most recently, Abdi et al. (2026) exhibit a single-sample matroid prophet inequality achieving an optimal competitive ratio of 1/21/2 when the order is adversarial yet fixed, and OpenAI (2026) achieve a constant competitive ratio with respect to the more powerful almighty adversary which adaptively chooses the arrival order.

One matter worth addressing is the relationship between prophet inequality problems and contention resolution. Indeed, for known prior distributions the problems are almost equivalent, with reductions in both directions Lee and Singla (2018).22 2 To be precise, the equivalence is with prophet inequalities measured against the ex-ante relaxation, which is a stronger benchmark than the expected offline optimum. One may therefore wonder whether our results can be obtained by reducing to the corresponding prophet (or prophet secretary) problem from samples. The answer is emphatically no. The reductions of Lee and Singla (2018) are sensitive to knowing the distribution, and our impossibility results for both single-sample, single-item and finite-sample, kk-uniform OCRSs serve to formally separate the two problems; in particular, a single sample permits a 1/21/2 prophet inequality, but not a 1/21/2-balanced OCRS.

2 Preliminaries

Let {1,…,n}\left\{1,\dots,n\right\} denote a ground set of elements, k≥1k\geq 1 be an integer capacity, and p=(p1,…,pn)∈[0,1]np=(p_{1},\dots,p_{n})\in[0,1]^{n} be an activation probability vector satisfying ∑i=1npi≤k\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\leq k. We sometimes use [n][n] to denote {1,…,n}\left\{1,\dots,n\right\}. A subset of [n][n] is feasible if it contains at most kk elements; this is a kk-uniform matroid constraint—also known as a cardinality constraint—with the single-item case corresponding to k=1k=1. We denote the kk-uniform matroid polytope by 𝒫k≔{x∈[0,1]n|∑i=1nxi≤k}\mathcal{P}_{k}\coloneqq\left\{x\in[0,1]^{n}\>\middle|\>\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\leq k\right\}. Let support​(p)≔{i∈[n]|pi>0}\text{support}(p)\coloneqq\left\{i\in[n]\>\middle|\>p_{i}>0\right\}.

Definition 2.1 (Contention Resolution Scheme).

An (offline) Contention Resolution Scheme (CRS) π\pi for the polytope 𝒫k\mathcal{P}_{k} is a procedure that, given a vector p∈𝒫kp\in\mathcal{P}_{k} and W⊆[n]W\subseteq[n], returns a random set πp​(W)⊆W∩support​(p)\pi_{p}(W)\subseteq W\cap\text{support}(p) such that |πp​(W)|≤k|\pi_{p}(W)|\leq k with probability 11, for all W⊆[n],p∈𝒫kW\subseteq[n],p\in\mathcal{P}_{k}. The scheme is said to be monotone if Pr[i∈πp(A1)]≥Pr[i∈πp(A2)]\Pr[i\in\pi_{p}(A_{1})]\geq\Pr[i\in\pi_{p}(A_{2})] for every i∈A1⊆A2i\in A_{1}\subseteq A_{2}.

Contention resolution schemes were introduced in Chekuri et al. (2014) as a tool for rounding fractional solutions for submodular maximization, though have found a variety of other uses since. Often pp denotes a fractional linear programming solution and we draw a random subset W⁡(p)W(p) of [n][n] where each i∈[n]i\in[n] appears independently with probability pip_{i}. The issue is that W⁡(p)W(p) might not be feasible for the given polytope. A CRS is then applied to W⁡(p)W(p) to return a set πp​(W⁡(p))⊆W⁡(p)\pi_{p}(W(p))\subseteq W(p) that is feasible with probability 11; in our case, this means it satisfies |πp​(W⁡(p))|≤k|\pi_{p}(W(p))|\leq k.

In the description above, π\pi is given all elements of W⁡(p)W(p) and can then choose πp​(W​(p))\pi_{p}(W(p)). Feldman, Svensson and Zenklusen Feldman et al. (2021) introduce an Online Contention Resolution Scheme (OCRS) where the random set W⁡(p)W(p) is obtained in the same way, but the indicator i∈W⁡(p)i\in W(p) is revealed sequentially to π\pi in an adversarial order fixed independently of the events i∈W⁡(p)i\in W(p), the samples and any internal randomness of π\pi. After each arrival, the OCRS has to immediately and irrevocably decide whether or not to accept i∈W⁡(p)i\in W(p) into πp​(W​(p))\pi_{p}(W(p)), subject to feasibility. Later, Adamczyk and Włodarczyk Adamczyk and Włodarczyk (2018) introduced Random Order Contention Resolution Schemes (ROCRSs) which are OCRSs with the arrival order chosen uniformly at random. We use Xi∼Ber⁡(pi)X_{i}\sim\operatorname{Ber}\left({p_{i}}\right), where Ber⁡(pi)\operatorname{Ber}\left({p_{i}}\right) denotes the Bernoulli distribution with success probability pip_{i}, to denote the random variable indicating whether or not i∈W⁡(p)i\in W(p). We call ii online-active if Xi=1X_{i}=1 and online-inactive otherwise.

In this work, we study ROCRSs and OCRSs that are given nn and kk, but not the activation probability vector pp. Instead, before observing the online activations, they receive mm samples per element for some m≥0m\geq 0. We write Yi(s)∼Ber⁡(pi)Y_{i}^{(s)}\sim\operatorname{Ber}\left({p_{i}}\right) for the ss-th sample of element ii. For a sample-based scheme on an arbitrary input set WW, we require the output to be a feasible subset of WW; we do not additionally require it to lie in support​(p)\text{support}(p). On the random input W⁡(p)W(p), the latter property holds automatically. A sample-based scheme is called monotone if Pr[i∈πp(A1)]≥Pr[i∈πp(A2)]\Pr[i\in\pi_{p}(A_{1})]\geq\Pr[i\in\pi_{p}(A_{2})] holds for all p∈𝒫kp\in\mathcal{P}_{k} and i∈A1⊆A2i\in A_{1}\subseteq A_{2}, when the samples Yj(ℓ)Y^{(\ell)}_{j} are independently drawn from Ber⁡(pj)\operatorname{Ber}\left({p_{j}}\right) for all j∈[n]j\in[n]. In the single-sample setting, we write YiY_{i} and call ii sample-active if Yi=1Y_{i}=1 and sample-inactive otherwise. All samples and online activations are mutually independent. For adversarial arrivals, we index elements in arrival order, without loss of generality, so the online observations are X1,…,XnX_{1},\dots,X_{n}. For random arrivals, indices identify fixed elements, rather than their positions in the arrival order.

Remark 2.1.

In the subsequent sections, whenever it simplifies our arguments, we assume that ∑i=1npi=k\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=k. As we show in Appendix C, all contention resolution schemes we design are monotone. Furthermore, we explain how we can add “dummy” elements to account for any missing mass for the random-order schemes, and why the assumption is justified by direct calculations for the adversarial-order schemes. Therefore, this assumption can be made without loss of generality.

3 The Single-Item Case

We start with the single-item case. Here, we show that a single sample suffices to design an optimal (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-balanced ROCRS (and thus also an offline CRS). We also show that this is not the case for adversarial arrivals, giving an impossibility of 0.4990.499. We then proceed to design an optimal 1/21/2-balanced OCRS using two samples per element, as well as a 0.480.48-balanced OCRS with one sample.

3.1 Random Order

We start with the random-order single-item case. Though we obtain a more general result for arbitrary kk in Section 4.1, the algorithm we present here, and its analysis, are appealing due to their simplicity. We prove the guarantee when ∑ipi=1\sum_{i}p_{i}=1; its extension to the case ∑ipi≤1\sum_{i}p_{i}\leq 1 is justified in Appendix C (see also Remark 2.1). As in Section 2, XiX_{i} indicates whether element ii is online-active, and YiY_{i} independently indicates whether it is sample-active.

Our single-item ROCRS is shown in Algorithm 1. For every online-active element ii, this ROCRS tosses an independent coin and accepts ii with some probability depending on the sample YiY_{i}. We prove the following.

Theorem 3.1.

For every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, (unknown) probability vector p∈[0,1]np\in[0,1]^{n} with ∑i=1npi=1\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=1, and every element i∈[n]i\in[n] with pi>0p_{i}>0, Algorithm 1 always accepts at most one element and satisfies

Ci≥1−1e.C_{i}\geq 1-\frac{1}{e}.

Feasibility is obvious by the algorithm’s description. Next, notice that the probability that element ii is online-active and its coin succeeds is pi​(1−pi/e)p_{i}(1-p_{i}/e). This implies an alternative description of the algorithm: it observes a sequence of independent Bernoulli random variables Z1,…,ZnZ_{1},\dots,Z_{n} where Zi∼Ber⁡(pi​(1−pi/e))Z_{i}\sim\operatorname{Ber}\left({p_{i}(1-p_{i}/e)}\right) and accepts the first ii such that Zi=1Z_{i}=1. Since the arrival order is uniformly random, the probability that we accept element ii, conditional on Xi=1X_{i}=1, can be written as

Ci=(1−pie)​𝔼​[11+∑j≠iZj],C_{i}=\left({1-\frac{p_{i}}{e}}\right)\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{1+\sum_{j\neq i}Z_{j}}\right],

since this is the probability that Zi=1Z_{i}=1 and ii arrives first from a sequence of 1+∑j≠iZj1+\sum_{j\neq i}Z_{j} ones.

Next, notice that if all pjp_{j} for j≠ij\neq i were close to 00, then ∑j≠iZj→Poi⁡(1−pi)\sum_{j\neq i}Z_{j}\to\operatorname{Poi}\left({1-p_{i}}\right), and the probability that ii is accepted conditional on Xi=1X_{i}=1 would be

(1−pie)​1−e−(1−pi)1−pi≥1−1e,\left({1-\frac{p_{i}}{e}}\right)\frac{1-e^{-(1-p_{i})}}{1-p_{i}}\geq 1-\frac{1}{e},

where the inequality follows from elementary manipulations, interpreting, at pi=1p_{i}=1, the fraction by its continuous value 11. Thus, it suffices to show that this is the worst case. In other words, it suffices to show that, for Zj′∼Poi⁡(pj)Z^{\prime}_{j}\sim\operatorname{Poi}\left({p_{j}}\right),

𝔼⁡[11+∑j≠iZj]≥𝔼⁡[11+∑j≠iZj′].\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{1+\sum_{j\neq i}Z_{j}}\right]\geq\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{1+\sum_{j\neq i}Z^{\prime}_{j}}\right]. (1)

By linearity of expectation, we have

3.2 Adversarial Order: Impossibility

Next, we construct a hard instance showing that, for adversarial arrivals and k=1k=1, there does not exist a single-sample 1/21/2-balanced OCRS. In the proof, we use the fact that for an OCRS π\pi to accept element ii, it has to first reach ii, and thus for every probability vector pp

Ci​(p)≤Pr⁡[Ri,π|Xi=1]=1−∑j<ipj​Cj​(p).C_{i}(p)\leq\Pr\left[R_{i,\pi}\>\middle|\>X_{i}=1\right]=1-\sum_{j<i}p_{j}C_{j}(p). (3)

Theorem 3.2.

There does not exist a single-sample, 1/21/2-balanced OCRS in the single-item setting, when the elements arrive in adversarial order.

3.3 Adversarial Order: Two-Sample 1/21/2-balanced OCRS

In this section, we use two independent samples Yi(1),Yi(2)∼Ber⁡(pi)Y_{i}^{(1)},Y_{i}^{(2)}\sim\operatorname{Ber}\left({p_{i}}\right) per element to design a 1/21/2-balanced OCRS for the single-item setting. We start with a useful reduction to a simple threshold construction.

Lemma 3.1.

Fix n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and a probability vector p∈[0,1]np\in[0,1]^{n} with ∑i=1npi=1\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=1. Let TT be a random variable independent of the online activations X1,…,XnX_{1},\dots,X_{n} that satisfies

Proof.

=12​∏ℓ=1i−1(1−pℓ)+12​∑j=1i−1pj​∏j<ℓ<i(1−pℓ)=12,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\prod_{\ell=1}^{i-1}(1-p_{\ell})+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}p_{j}\prod_{j<\ell<i}(1-p_{\ell})=\frac{1}{2},

where the last equality follows from the fact that ∏ℓ=1i−1(1−pℓ)\prod_{\ell=1}^{i-1}(1-p_{\ell}) is the probability that none of the first i−1i-1 elements are active, and pj​∏j<ℓ<i(1−pℓ)p_{j}\prod_{j<\ell<i}(1-p_{\ell}) is the probability that the jjth element is the last active element among the first i−1i-1, which are mutually exclusive and exhaustive events. ∎

By Lemma 3.1 if, using only the samples, we can construct a threshold T∈{0,1,…,n}T\in\left\{0,1,\dots,n\right\} such that

Pr[T=0]=12,andPr[T=i]=pi2for every i∈[n],\Pr[T=0]=\frac{1}{2},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Pr[T=i]=\frac{p_{i}}{2}\qquad\text{for every }i\in[n],

the result follows. Next, we show how to construct such a threshold by reducing it in turn to the design of a single-sample offline CRS with certain guarantees, with the first set of samples playing the role of online arrivals and the second set of samples serving as samples. In more detail, we choose TT by applying a modified version of the (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-balanced (offline) CRS of Feige and Vondrák (Feige and Vondrák, 2010, Section 1.2) to {i|Yi(1)=1}\left\{i\>\middle|\>Y_{i}^{(1)}=1\right\}, which we also implement using only a single sample per element – in this case the Yi(2)Y^{(2)}_{i}’s. Our final OCRS simply accepts the first online-active element strictly after TT.

Theorem 3.3.

For every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and (unknown) probability vector p∈[0,1]np\in[0,1]^{n} with ∑i=1npi=1\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=1, the threshold TT in Algorithm 2 satisfies

Pr[T=0]=12,andPr[T=i]=pi2for every i∈[n].\Pr[T=0]=\frac{1}{2},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Pr[T=i]=\frac{p_{i}}{2}\qquad\text{for every }i\in[n].

Below, we analyze Algorithm 2 using the Feige and Vondrák (offline) CRS (Feige and Vondrák, 2010, Section 1.2) as a black-box and describe the main ideas behind the proof of Theorem 3.3. The formal proof of the theorem is self-contained and can be found in Appendix A.4.

For i∈[n]i\in[n] and S⊆[n]S\subseteq[n], let

(1−pi)Pr[𝒮={i}]=(1−pi)pi∏j≠i(1−pj)=pi∏j=1n(1−pj)=piPr[𝒮=∅].(1-p_{i})\Pr[\mathcal{S}=\left\{i\right\}]=(1-p_{i})p_{i}\prod_{j\neq i}(1-p_{j})=p_{i}\prod_{j=1}^{n}(1-p_{j})=p_{i}\Pr[\mathcal{S}=\emptyset].

Finally, since T∈{0,1,…,n}T\in\left\{0,1,\dots,n\right\} and ∑i=1npi=1\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=1, we have Pr[T=0]=1−∑i=1nPr[T=i]=1−(1/2)∑i=1npi=1/2\Pr[T=0]=1-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Pr[T=i]=1-(1/2)\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=1/2.

3.4 Adversarial Order: Single-Sample 0.480.48-balanced OCRS

Next, we design a single-sample, 0.480.48-balanced OCRS for the single-item setting and adversarial arrivals. The idea behind our OCRS is to use the samples to construct a threshold TT that is close to the ideal one that satisfies Pr[T=0]=1/2\Pr[T=0]=1/2 and Pr[T=i]=pi/2\Pr[T=i]=p_{i}/2.

εi≔pi2−Pr[T=i]≥0,\varepsilon_{i}\coloneqq\frac{p_{i}}{2}-\Pr[T=i]\geq 0,

gℓ​(t)={∏t<j<ℓ(1−pj),0≤t<ℓ,0,ℓ≤t≤n.g_{\ell}(t)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\prod_{t<j<\ell}(1-p_{j}),&0\leq t<\ell,\\ 0,&\ell\leq t\leq n.\end{cases}

It follows that

Cℓ=𝔼⁡[gℓ​(T)],and𝔼⁡[gℓ​(T∗)]=12,C_{\ell}=\mathbb{E}[g_{\ell}(T)],\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{E}[g_{\ell}(T^{*})]=\frac{1}{2},

εi≤1−1/e12​pi​(1−pi).\varepsilon_{i}\leq\frac{1-1/e}{12}\>p_{i}(1-p_{i}).

4 General kk

We continue with the cardinality case for general k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. Here we show that, perhaps surprisingly, for uniformly random arrivals a single sample suffices to obtain an optimal (1−e−k​kk/k!)(1-e^{-k}k^{k}/k!)-balanced ROCRS (and thus also offline CRS) for every kk, generalizing our result from Section 3.1. We then move on to adversarial arrivals. Even though a single sample does not suffice for an optimal OCRS for k=1k=1, we show that, for general kk, a single sample does suffice to obtain an asymptotically optimal 1−O⁡(1/k)1-O\left({1/\sqrt{k}}\right)-balanced OCRS.

4.1 Random Order

We start with the random order case. The ROCRS we design, shown in Algorithm 4, is surprisingly simple: greedily accept the first k−1k-1 online-active elements and when observing the kk-th online-active element ii, if Yi=0Y_{i}=0, accept it. Else, if Yi=1Y_{i}=1, accept ii with probability (k+1)/(2​k+1)(k+1)/(2k+1), else reject it and greedily accept the next online-active element. We call this the Almost-Greedy ROCRS. Notice that it satisfies an interesting property: it only ever looks at a single sample YiY_{i}, but it cannot a priori know which YiY_{i} is the useful one so it needs a sample per element. We prove the following.

Theorem 4.1.

For every n,k∈ℕn,k\in\mathbb{N}, (unknown) probability vector p∈[0,1]np\in[0,1]^{n} with ∑i=1npi=k\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=k and every element i∈[n]i\in[n] with pi>0p_{i}>0, Algorithm 4 always accepts at most kk elements and satisfies

Ci≥1−e−k​kkk!.C_{i}\geq 1-e^{-k}\frac{k^{k}}{k!}.
Proof.

Feasibility follows easily from the algorithm’s description. Fix an element ii with pi>0p_{i}>0, and let S−i=∑j≠iXjS_{-i}=\sum_{j\neq i}X_{j} be the number of other online-active elements. First we analyze the greedy rule which accepts the first kk online-active elements, before comparing our algorithm to this rule in order to lower-bound CiC_{i}.

Condition on Xi=1X_{i}=1 and on the other online activations {Xj}j≠i\left\{X_{j}\right\}_{j\neq i}. The arrival order of the S−i+1S_{-i}+1 online-active elements is uniformly random, so each possible rank of ii has probability 1/(S−i+1)1/(S_{-i}+1). ARk⁡(s)≔min⁡{1,ks+1}.\operatorname{AR}_{k}(s)\coloneqq\min\left\{1,\frac{k}{s+1}\right\}.

4.2 Adversarial Order

We continue with the adversarial order case. Without loss of generality, let 1,…,n1,\dots,n be the arrival order and pp be a probability vector such that ∑i=1npi≤k\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\leq k. The idea behind our OCRS, shown in Algorithm 5, is the following: for each online-active element, we call it a candidate if it passes a certain count test, maintaining a counter CC of candidates seen and a counter AA of number of accepted elements. Afterwards, we accept every candidate with a certain probability that changes as the algorithm progresses, depending on CC and AA. We call this the Count Test OCRS.

The OCRS we design is closely related to that of Dinev and Weinberg Dinev and Weinberg (2024) for known activation probabilities. However, it differs in a few ways. First, our algorithm uses a random RR instead of fixing it at k\sqrt{k} as in Dinev and Weinberg (2024). Second, the acceptance probability of our algorithm changes as CC and AA change, instead of being fixed at 1−1/k1-1/\sqrt{k} as in Dinev and Weinberg (2024). Third, we frame the algorithm in terms of a running count of candidates and have a slightly different acceptance rule than that of Dinev and Weinberg (2024).

All of these three changes are actually not necessary: we can simply use R=⌊k⌋R=\left\lfloor\sqrt{k}\right\rfloor deterministically, we can accept at a flat rate of min⁡{1,(k−k)/N}\min\left\{1,(k-\sqrt{k})/N\right\} until we run out of space and we can also remove the candidates and set q=1q=1 if N=RN=R and q=min⁡{1,(k−k)/(N−R)}q=\min\left\{1,(k-\sqrt{k})/{(N-R)}\right\} otherwise, accepting an online-active element ii with probability qq only if A+1≤R+q​∑j≤iYjA+1\leq R+q\sum_{j\leq i}Y_{j}; this is exactly equivalent to the OCRS of Dinev and Weinberg (2024), with the (unknown) pip_{i}’s replaced by the YiY_{i}’s. All these changes, however, significantly simplify the analysis and thus were made for the sake of clarity of exposition.

Theorem 4.2.

For every n,k∈ℕn,k\in\mathbb{N}, integer r≥1r\geq 1, (unknown) probability vector p∈[0,1]np\in[0,1]^{n} with ∑i=1npi≤k\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\leq k and every element i∈[n]i\in[n] with pi>0p_{i}>0, Algorithm 5 always accepts at most kk elements and satisfies

Ci≥1−1r+1−r2​k−12​k.C_{i}\geq 1-\frac{1}{r+1}-\frac{r}{2k}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{k}}.

Before we prove the theorem, observe that, for r=⌊2​k⌋r=\left\lfloor\sqrt{2k}\right\rfloor, the guarantee becomes

Ci≥1−2+1/2k=1−O⁡(1k).C_{i}\geq 1-\frac{\sqrt{2}+1/2}{\sqrt{k}}=1-O\left({\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}}\right).
Proof of Theorem 4.2.

We first give an equivalent description of the acceptance rule in Algorithm 5. Condition on RR, the samples, and the online activations. The list of candidates is then fixed, since the count test does not depend on the acceptance decisions. Moreover, the count test ensures that there are at most N=R+∑j=1nYjN=R+\sum_{j=1}^{n}Y_{j} candidates.

Consider choosing min⁡{k,N}\min\left\{k,N\right\} of the NN possible candidate positions uniformly at random, and accepting each candidate exactly when its position is chosen. Any chosen positions beyond the end of the list are unused. After processing CC candidates, of which AA were accepted, there are N−CN-C positions left, of which min⁡{k,N}−A\min\left\{k,N\right\}-A are chosen. Conditional on the choices for the first CC positions, the chosen positions among the remaining ones are still uniformly distributed. Thus, the conditional probability of accepting the next candidate is

min⁡{k,N}−AN−C,\frac{\min\left\{k,N\right\}-A}{N-C},

which is exactly the acceptance probability in Algorithm 5. This description shows that the acceptance probabilities are well-defined and that the algorithm accepts at most kk elements. If N=0N=0, the count test admits no candidates and no acceptance decision is needed.

Fix an element ii with pi>0p_{i}>0. Conditional on Xi=1X_{i}=1, the algorithm rejects ii either because it fails the count test or because it is a candidate whose position is not chosen. We first use the description above to bound the probability of the latter event.

For fixed RR, samples, and online activations, the position of each candidate is fixed, while each of the NN positions is equally likely to be chosen. Since exactly min⁡{k,N}\min\left\{k,N\right\} positions are chosen, each candidate is accepted with probability min⁡{k,N}/N\min\left\{k,N\right\}/N. Therefore, when N≤kN\leq k, every candidate is accepted, while for N>kN>k the rejection probability is

1−kN=N−kN≤N−kk.1-\frac{k}{N}=\frac{N-k}{N}\leq\frac{N-k}{k}.

Overall, for every fixed realization of RR, the samples, and the online activations, this rejection probability is at most (N−k)+/k(N-k)^{+}/k. Averaging over RR, the samples, and the other online activations gives

Pr⁡[{i​ is a candidate}∩Aic|Xi=1]≤1k​𝔼​[(N−k)+|Xi=1]=1k​𝔼​[(N−k)+].\Pr\left[\left\{i\text{ is a candidate}\right\}\cap A_{i}^{c}\>\middle|\>X_{i}=1\right]\leq\frac{1}{k}\mathbb{E}\left[(N-k)^{+}\>\middle|\>X_{i}=1\right]=\frac{1}{k}\mathbb{E}\left[(N-k)^{+}\right].

Taking also into account the probability that ii fails the count test, we obtain

1−Ci≤Pr⁡[i​ is not a candidate|Xi=1]+1k​𝔼​[(N−k)+].1-C_{i}\leq\Pr\left[i\text{ is not a candidate}\>\middle|\>X_{i}=1\right]+\frac{1}{k}\mathbb{E}\left[(N-k)^{+}\right]. (8)

Thus, it suffices to bound the probability of failing the count test and the expected value of (N−k)+(N-k)^{+}.

Otherwise, the number of candidates does not change. Therefore,

B0=R,andBt=(Bt−1+Yt−Xt)+for ​t>0.B_{0}=R,\qquad\text{and}\qquad B_{t}=(B_{t-1}+Y_{t}-X_{t})^{+}\qquad\text{for }t>0.

5 Sample Complexity

Next, we investigate whether the samples used by our schemes are necessary to obtain optimal guarantees. For random arrivals, the answer depends on kk: one sample per element is necessary for k∈{1,2,3,4}k\in\left\{1,2,3,4\right\}, whereas no samples are needed for k≥5k\geq 5. The latter fact follows directly from a lemma by Arnosti and Ma Arnosti and Ma (2021). Perhaps surprisingly, for adversarial arrivals and every fixed k≥2k\geq 2, we show that no fixed finite number of samples per element suffices to attain the optimal guarantee for known activation probabilities.

5.1 Random Order

We start with the random order case. Consider the greedy rule that accepts the first kk online-active elements. Clearly, this rule uses no samples and does not need to know pp. The following guarantee is a direct consequence of (Arnosti and Ma, 2021, Lemma 6).

Corollary 5.1.

For every n,k≥1n,k\geq 1, probability vector p∈[0,1]np\in[0,1]^{n} with ∑i=1npi≤k\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\leq k, and element ii with pi>0p_{i}>0, the ROCRS that greedily accepts the first kk active elements satisfies

Ci≥min⁡{kk+1, 1−e−k​kkk!}.C_{i}\geq\min\left\{\frac{k}{k+1},\;1-e^{-k}\frac{k^{k}}{k!}\right\}.

In particular, it is an optimal (1−e−k​kk/k!)(1-e^{-k}k^{k}/k!)-balanced ROCRS for k≥5k\geq 5.

Proof.

Firstly, the set returned by the ROCRS is trivially feasible. Assume that ∑i=1npi=k\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=k, and let S=∑j=1nXjS=\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_{j} and S−i=∑j≠iXjS_{-i}=\sum_{j\neq i}X_{j}. By (Arnosti and Ma, 2021, Lemma 6), for every sum SS of independent Bernoulli random variables with mean kk, we have

𝔼⁡[ARk⁡(S)]≥min⁡{kk+1, 1−e−k​kkk!}.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{AR}_{k}(S)]\geq\min\left\{\frac{k}{k+1},\;1-e^{-k}\frac{k^{k}}{k!}\right\}.

Conditional on Xi=1X_{i}=1 and the other online activations, the rank of ii among the S−i+1S_{-i}+1 online-active elements is uniform. Thus, using the fact that ARk\operatorname{AR}_{k} is non-increasing,

Ci=𝔼⁡[ARk⁡(S−i)]≥𝔼⁡[ARk⁡(S)]≥min⁡{kk+1, 1−e−k​kkk!}.C_{i}=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{AR}_{k}(S_{-i})]\geq\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{AR}_{k}(S)]\geq\min\left\{\frac{k}{k+1},\;1-e^{-k}\frac{k^{k}}{k!}\right\}.

Finally, if ∑ipi<k\sum_{i}p_{i}<k, we can simply add independent Bernoulli random variables to SS such that 𝔼⁡[S]=k\mathbb{E}[S]=k. Since ARk\operatorname{AR}_{k} is non-increasing, this can only decrease 𝔼⁡[ARk⁡(S)]\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{AR}_{k}(S)], and thus the same bound follows. ∎

For k∈{1,2,3,4}k\in\left\{1,2,3,4\right\}, we have k/(k+1)<1−e−k​kk/k!k/(k+1)<1-e^{-k}k^{k}/k!, whereas the inequality is reversed for k≥5k\geq 5. Next, we show that the guarantee in Corollary 5.1 is tight for schemes with no samples, even in the offline setting. Together with Theorem 4.1, this characterizes exactly the minimum number of samples per element needed for an optimal ROCRS: one for k∈{1,2,3,4}k\in\left\{1,2,3,4\right\} and zero for k≥5k\geq 5.

Proposition 5.1.

Fix an integer k≥1k\geq 1. If an ROCRS (respectively, an offline CRS) that uses no samples is cc-balanced uniformly over all ground-set sizes and all p∈𝒫kp\in\mathcal{P}_{k}, then

c≤min⁡{kk+1, 1−e−k​kkk!}.c\leq\min\left\{\frac{k}{k+1},\;1-e^{-k}\frac{k^{k}}{k!}\right\}.
Proof.

First we show that c≤k/(k+1)c\leq k/(k+1). Let n=k+1n=k+1. Whenever all elements are online-active, feasibility implies that some element is accepted with probability at most k/(k+1)k/(k+1); let ii be this element. Since π\pi receives no samples and does not know pp, it is the same for every probability vector p∈(0,1]np\in(0,1]^{n}.

For ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), consider

Ci≤kk+1​(1−εk)k+1−(1−εk)k=1−1k+1​(1−εk)k≤k+εk+1,C_{i}\leq\frac{k}{k+1}\left({1-\frac{\varepsilon}{k}}\right)^{k}+1-\left({1-\frac{\varepsilon}{k}}\right)^{k}=1-\frac{1}{k+1}\left({1-\frac{\varepsilon}{k}}\right)^{k}\leq\frac{k+\varepsilon}{k+1},

For the other upper bound, consider n≥kn\geq k elements with pi=k/np_{i}=k/n for every i∈[n]i\in[n], and let S=∑i=1nXi∼Bin⁡(n,k/n)S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\sim\operatorname{Bin}\left({n,k/n}\right). Suppose that π\pi is cc-balanced for some c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1]. Then,

c​k≤∑i=1nPr⁡[Ai]≤𝔼⁡[min⁡{k,S}],ck\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Pr[A_{i}]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\min\left\{k,S\right\}\right],

where the second inequality follows from the fact that π\pi has to output a feasible set. As n→∞n\to\infty, SS converges in distribution to Z∼Poi⁡(k)Z\sim\operatorname{Poi}\left({k}\right). Taking the limit and using (6) yields

5.2 Adversarial Order

We continue with adversarial arrivals. As shown in Section 3.3, two samples per element suffice to recover the optimal 1/21/2-balanced OCRS for k=1k=1. We show that for k≥2k\geq 2 even an arbitrarily large fixed number of samples per element does not suffice to attain the optimal guarantee for known activation probabilities.

Fix an integer k≥2k\geq 2. We use γ\gamma (and drop the dependency on kk) to denote the optimal guarantee of an OCRS that knows pp, uniformly over all nn and all probability vectors with ∑ipi=k\sum_{i}p_{i}=k; this is characterized for every kk by Jiang, Ma, and Zhang Jiang et al. (2023).

where the limit follows from (13) and Pr1⁡[En]→0\Pr_{1}[E_{n}]\to 0. This contradicts the positive lower bound in (12). ∎

The same argument gives a positive gap from γ\gamma for each fixed sample bound. For k=1k=1, we have γ=1/2\gamma=1/2 and t2=1=kt_{2}=1=k, so the choice a<t2<b<ka<t_{2}<b<k is impossible, which is why there exists an optimal two-sample OCRS like the one we present in Section 3.3.

Corollary 5.2.

For every fixed k≥2k\geq 2 and finite m≥0m\geq 0, there is εk,m>0\varepsilon_{k,m}>0 such that every OCRS using at most mm samples per element has worst-case balancedness at most γ−εk,m\gamma-\varepsilon_{k,m}, even on instances with ∑ipi=k\sum_{i}p_{i}=k.

Proof.

Suppose, towards contradiction, that there is a sequence of OCRSs with balancedness guarantees cr→γc_{r}\to\gamma, all using at most mm samples per element. Apply the rr-th OCRS to the two instances above with block size nr→∞n_{r}\to\infty. The inequalities for a fixed instance in the proof of Lemma 5.1 hold with crc_{r} in place of γ\gamma. Since cr→γc_{r}\to\gamma, taking the limit gives the same inequalities for HℓH_{\ell} and the same bound Hk​(k)≤1−γH_{k}(k)\leq 1-\gamma. That proof therefore still gives (12). The second moments in (13) remain bounded because mm is fixed, and the same Cauchy–Schwarz argument that yields a contradiction still holds. ∎

A.4 A Self-Contained Proof of Theorem 3.3

Theorem 3.3.

For every p∈[0,1]np\in[0,1]^{n} with ∑i=1npi=1\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=1, the threshold TT in Algorithm 2 satisfies

+12​Pr⁡[J≠i∧YJ(2)=1∧J′=i|𝒮−i≠∅]\displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{2}\Pr\left[J\neq i\wedge Y^{(2)}_{J}=1\wedge J^{\prime}=i\>\middle|\>\mathcal{S}-i\neq\emptyset\right] (16)

Fix SS with i∈Si\in S and |S|≥2|S|\geq 2, and condition on 𝒮=S\mathcal{S}=S. The choice of JJ is uniformly random from SS and, conditional on J=jJ=j, the choice J′J^{\prime} is uniform on S−jS-j. 1−pi|S|+∑j∈S−i1|S|⋅pj|S|−1\displaystyle\frac{1-p_{i}}{|S|}+\sum_{j\in S-i}\frac{1}{|S|}\cdot\frac{p_{j}}{|S|-1} =1|S|​(∑j∉Spj+∑j∈S−ipj)+∑j∈S−i1|S|⋅pj|S|−1\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|S|}\left({\sum_{j\notin S}p_{j}+\sum_{j\in S-i}p_{j}}\right)+\sum_{j\in S-i}\frac{1}{|S|}\cdot\frac{p_{j}}{|S|-1}
=1|S|​∑j∉Spj+∑j∈S−ipj|S|​(1+1|S|−1)=1|S|​∑j∉Spj+∑j∈S−ipj|S|​|S||S|−1\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{j\notin S}p_{j}+\sum_{j\in S-i}\frac{p_{j}}{|S|}\left({1+\frac{1}{|S|-1}}\right)=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{j\notin S}p_{j}+\sum_{j\in S-i}\frac{p_{j}}{|S|}\frac{|S|}{|S|-1}

where the first equality follows from the fact that ∑j=1npj=1\sum_{j=1}^{n}p_{j}=1. Therefore,

=12​∑j≠ipj​𝔼​[1|𝒮−i−j|+1|𝒮−i≠∅].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j\neq i}p_{j}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}-i-j|+1}\>\middle|\>\mathcal{S}-i\neq\emptyset\right].

Combining both cases and averaging over their original distributions gives

+12Pr[𝒮−i≠∅]∑j≠ipj𝔼[1|𝒮−i−j|+1|𝒮−i≠∅]\displaystyle\qquad+\frac{1}{2}\Pr[\mathcal{S}-i\neq\emptyset]\sum_{j\neq i}p_{j}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}-i-j|+1}\>\middle|\>\mathcal{S}-i\neq\emptyset\right]

Appendix B An Alternative Optimal ROCRS

In this section we give an alternative ROCRS with the same optimal balancedness as in Theorem 4.1. Before that, we start with some definitions.

Definition B.1 (Poisson binomial distribution).

The Poisson binomial distribution PB⁡(p1,…,pn)\operatorname{PB}\left({p_{1},\dots,p_{n}}\right) is the distribution of a sum of independent Bernoulli random variables with success probabilities p1,…,pnp_{1},\dots,p_{n}. We also write such a sum as ∑j=1nBer⁡(pj)\sum_{j=1}^{n}\operatorname{Ber}\left({p_{j}}\right), and use the same convention for sums of independent Poisson random variables.

Definition B.2 (Discrete differences and convexity).

For a function f:ℕ→ℝf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}, let

Δ​f​(n)≔f⁡(n+1)−f⁡(n),andΔ2​f​(n)≔Δ​f​(n+1)−Δ​f​(n).\Delta f(n)\coloneqq f(n+1)-f(n),\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Delta^{2}f(n)\coloneqq\Delta f(n+1)-\Delta f(n).

The function ff is convex if Δ2​f​(n)≥0\Delta^{2}f(n)\geq 0 for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, and concave if Δ2​f​(n)≤0\Delta^{2}f(n)\leq 0 for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}.

Definition B.3 (Convex order).

For random variables X,YX,Y supported on ℕ\mathbb{N} with finite means, we say that XX dominates YY in convex order, and write X≥c​xYX\geq_{cx}Y, if

𝔼⁡[f⁡(X)]≥𝔼⁡[f⁡(Y)]\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\geq\mathbb{E}[f(Y)]

for every convex function f:ℕ→ℝf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R} for which both expectations are finite.

For our alternative proof of Theorem 4.1, we need the following characterization of stochastic convex order.

B.1 Characterization of Convex Order

In this section, we generalize the following consequence of Hoeffding’s theorem for Poisson binomial random variables [22].

Theorem B.1 (Hoeffding, [22]).

Let X∼Poi⁡(λ)X\sim\operatorname{Poi}\left({\lambda}\right) and Y∼PB⁡(p1,…,pn)Y\sim\operatorname{PB}\left({p_{1},\dots,p_{n}}\right), where λ=∑i=1npi\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}. Then, for every convex f:ℕ→ℝf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R} we have

𝔼⁡[f⁡(X)]≥𝔼⁡[f⁡(Y)],\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\geq\mathbb{E}[f(Y)],

and the inequality is reversed if ff is concave.

We generalize the above theorem in three ways:

  1. 1.

    We allow XX and YY to have different means.

  2. 2.

    We allow XX and YY to follow arbitrary distributions on ℕ\mathbb{N}.

  3. 3.

    We allow for an arbitrary ff that is neither convex nor concave, provided it satisfies a mild second-order condition.

Under the above assumptions, we characterize the exact conditions under which: (i) 𝔼⁡[f⁡(X)]≥𝔼⁡[f⁡(Y)]\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\geq\mathbb{E}[f(Y)] and (ii) X≥c​xYX\geq_{cx}Y, for all such X,YX,Y and ff. In what follows, for two random variables X,YX,Y with finite mean, let

δ≔𝔼⁡[X]−𝔼⁡[Y]andDn≔𝔼⁡[(X−n−1)+]−𝔼⁡[(Y−n−1)+],n∈ℕ.\delta\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[Y]\qquad\text{and}\qquad D_{n}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[(X-n-1)^{+}]-\mathbb{E}[(Y-n-1)^{+}],\quad n\in\mathbb{N}.
Theorem B.2.

Let X,YX,Y be random variables with finite mean, supported on ℕ\mathbb{N}, δ≔𝔼⁡[X]−𝔼⁡[Y]\delta\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[Y] and Dn≔𝔼⁡[(X−n−1)+]−𝔼⁡[(Y−n−1)+]D_{n}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[(X-n-1)^{+}]-\mathbb{E}[(Y-n-1)^{+}] for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. Then, for all functions f:ℕ→ℝf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R} with

∑n≥0(𝔼⁡[(X−n−1)+]+𝔼⁡[(Y−n−1)+])​|Δ2​f​(n)|<∞,\sum_{n\geq 0}\left({\mathbb{E}[(X-n-1)^{+}]+\mathbb{E}[(Y-n-1)^{+}]}\right)\left|\Delta^{2}f(n)\right|<\infty,

we have

𝔼⁡[f⁡(X)]−𝔼⁡[f⁡(Y)]=δ​Δ​f​(0)+∑n≥0Dn​Δ2​f​(n).\mathbb{E}[f(X)]-\mathbb{E}[f(Y)]=\delta\Delta f(0)+\sum_{n\geq 0}D_{n}\Delta^{2}f(n).
Proof.

Note that, for all m≥0m\geq 0,

f⁡(m)−f⁡(0)=∑i=0m−1(f⁡(i+1)−f⁡(i))=∑i=0m−1Δ​f​(i).f(m)-f(0)=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\left({f(i+1)-f(i)}\right)=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\Delta f(i). (24)

Since Δ2​f​(i)=Δ​f​(i+1)−Δ​f​(i)\Delta^{2}f(i)=\Delta f(i+1)-\Delta f(i), we have

Δ​f​(i)−Δ​f​(0)=∑n=0i−1(Δ​f​(n+1)−Δ​f​(n))=∑n=0i−1Δ2​f​(n),\Delta f(i)-\Delta f(0)=\sum_{n=0}^{i-1}\left({\Delta f(n+1)-\Delta f(n)}\right)=\sum_{n=0}^{i-1}\Delta^{2}f(n),

and thus

∑i=0m−1Δ​f​(i)=m​Δ​f​(0)+∑i=0m−1∑n=0i−1Δ2​f​(n).\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\Delta f(i)=m\Delta f(0)+\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\sum_{n=0}^{i-1}\Delta^{2}f(n).

Substituting the above expression into (24) gives

f⁡(m)\displaystyle f(m) =f⁡(0)+m​Δ​f​(0)+∑i=0m−1∑n=0i−1Δ2​f​(n).\displaystyle=f(0)+m\Delta f(0)+\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\sum_{n=0}^{i-1}\Delta^{2}f(n).

For a fixed n≤m−2n\leq m-2, the term Δ2​f​(n)\Delta^{2}f(n) occurs in the double sum exactly m−n−1m-n-1 times, once for each i=n+1,n+2,…,m−1i=n+1,n+2,\dots,m-1. Thus, for all m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N},

f⁡(m)=f⁡(0)+m​Δ​f​(0)+∑n≥0(m−n−1)+​Δ2​f​(n).f(m)=f(0)+m\Delta f(0)+\sum_{n\geq 0}(m-n-1)^{+}\Delta^{2}f(n). (25)

Therefore,

𝔼⁡[f⁡(X)]=f⁡(0)+𝔼⁡[X]​Δ​f​(0)+𝔼⁡[∑n≥0(X−n−1)+​Δ2​f​(n)]\mathbb{E}[f(X)]=f(0)+\mathbb{E}[X]\Delta f(0)+\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{n\geq 0}(X-n-1)^{+}\Delta^{2}f(n)\right] (26)

and

𝔼⁡[f⁡(Y)]=f⁡(0)+𝔼⁡[Y]​Δ​f​(0)+𝔼⁡[∑n≥0(Y−n−1)+​Δ2​f​(n)].\mathbb{E}[f(Y)]=f(0)+\mathbb{E}[Y]\Delta f(0)+\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{n\geq 0}(Y-n-1)^{+}\Delta^{2}f(n)\right]. (27)

Subtracting (27) from (26) yields

𝔼⁡[f⁡(X)]−𝔼⁡[f⁡(Y)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[f(X)]-\mathbb{E}[f(Y)] =δ​Δ​f​(0)+𝔼⁡[∑n≥0((X−n−1)+−(Y−n−1)+)​Δ2​f​(n)]\displaystyle=\delta\Delta f(0)+\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{n\geq 0}\left({(X-n-1)^{+}-(Y-n-1)^{+}}\right)\Delta^{2}f(n)\right]
=δ​Δ​f​(0)+∑n≥0𝔼⁡[(X−n−1)+−(Y−n−1)+]​Δ2​f​(n)\displaystyle=\delta\Delta f(0)+\sum_{n\geq 0}\mathbb{E}\left[(X-n-1)^{+}-(Y-n-1)^{+}\right]\Delta^{2}f(n)
=δ​Δ​f​(0)+∑n≥0Dn​Δ2​f​(n),\displaystyle=\delta\Delta f(0)+\sum_{n\geq 0}D_{n}\Delta^{2}f(n),

where the second equality follows from the assumption that

∑n≥0(𝔼⁡[(X−n−1)+]+𝔼⁡[(Y−n−1)+])​|Δ2​f​(n)|<∞.∎\sum_{n\geq 0}\left({\mathbb{E}[(X-n-1)^{+}]+\mathbb{E}[(Y-n-1)^{+}]}\right)\left|\Delta^{2}f(n)\right|<\infty.\qed

Theorem B.2 gives a simple characterization of the random variables and functions for which 𝔼⁡[f⁡(X)]≥𝔼⁡[f⁡(Y)]\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\geq\mathbb{E}[f(Y)], under a mild assumption on ff. It also yields the following characterization of convex order domination.

Theorem B.3.

Let X,YX,Y be random variables with finite means, supported on ℕ\mathbb{N}. The following are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    X≥c​xYX\geq_{cx}Y.

  2. 2.

    δ=0\delta=0 and Dn≥0D_{n}\geq 0 for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}.

Proof.

First, assume that X≥c​xYX\geq_{cx}Y. The functions f⁡(Z)=Zf(Z)=Z and g⁡(Z)=−Zg(Z)=-Z are both convex, and together imply that

{𝔼⁡[X]≥𝔼⁡[Y]𝔼⁡[X]≤𝔼⁡[Y]⟹𝔼⁡[X]=𝔼⁡[Y]⇔δ=0.\begin{cases}\mathbb{E}[X]\geq\mathbb{E}[Y]\\ \mathbb{E}[X]\leq\mathbb{E}[Y]\end{cases}\implies\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}[Y]\iff\delta=0.

Furthermore, the function hn​(Z)=(Z−n−1)+h_{n}(Z)=(Z-n-1)^{+} is also convex for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, and thus 𝔼⁡[hn​(X)]≥𝔼⁡[hn​(Y)]\mathbb{E}[h_{n}(X)]\geq\mathbb{E}[h_{n}(Y)], which implies Dn≥0D_{n}\geq 0.

Next, assume that δ=0\delta=0 and Dn≥0D_{n}\geq 0 for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. Let f:ℕ→ℝf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R} be convex. As in the proof of Theorem B.2, we have

f⁡(n)−f⁡(0)−n​Δ​f​(0)=∑m≥0(n−m−1)+​Δ2​f​(m),f(n)-f(0)-n\Delta f(0)=\sum_{m\geq 0}(n-m-1)^{+}\Delta^{2}f(m),

and thus

𝔼⁡[f⁡(Y)]−f⁡(0)−𝔼⁡[Y]​Δ​f​(0)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[f(Y)]-f(0)-\mathbb{E}[Y]\Delta f(0) =∑m≥0𝔼⁡[(Y−m−1)+]​Δ2​f​(m)\displaystyle=\sum_{m\geq 0}\mathbb{E}[(Y-m-1)^{+}]\Delta^{2}f(m)
≤∑m≥0𝔼⁡[(X−m−1)+]​Δ2​f​(m)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{m\geq 0}\mathbb{E}[(X-m-1)^{+}]\Delta^{2}f(m)
=𝔼⁡[f⁡(X)]−f⁡(0)−𝔼⁡[X]​Δ​f​(0),\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[f(X)]-f(0)-\mathbb{E}[X]\Delta f(0),

where the inequality follows from Dn≥0D_{n}\geq 0. Since δ=0\delta=0, we have 𝔼⁡[X]=𝔼⁡[Y]\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}[Y], and thus 𝔼⁡[f⁡(Y)]≤𝔼⁡[f⁡(X)]\mathbb{E}[f(Y)]\leq\mathbb{E}[f(X)]. ∎

Therefore, Theorem B.3 recovers Theorem B.1 as a corollary: since λ=∑i=1npi\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}, we have 𝔼⁡[X]=𝔼⁡[Y]⟹δ=0\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}[Y]\implies\delta=0. Fix an integer r≥0r\geq 0, and let

Vi=∑j=1iPoi⁡(pj)+∑j=i+1nBer⁡(pj).V_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{i}\operatorname{Poi}\left({p_{j}}\right)+\sum_{j=i+1}^{n}\operatorname{Ber}\left({p_{j}}\right).

Thus, VnV_{n} has the same distribution as XX by the additivity of Poisson random variables, and V0V_{0} has the same distribution as YY. For i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n, let Wi=∑j=1i−1Poi⁡(pj)+∑j=i+1nBer⁡(pj)W_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\operatorname{Poi}\left({p_{j}}\right)+\sum_{j=i+1}^{n}\operatorname{Ber}\left({p_{j}}\right), and notice that

𝔼⁡[(Vi−r−1)+]−𝔼⁡[(Vi−1−r−1)+]=𝔼⁡[(Poi⁡(pi)+Wi−r−1)+]−𝔼⁡[(Ber⁡(pi)+Wi−r−1)+].\mathbb{E}[(V_{i}-r-1)^{+}]-\mathbb{E}[(V_{i-1}-r-1)^{+}]=\mathbb{E}\left[\left({\operatorname{Poi}\left({p_{i}}\right)+W_{i}-r-1}\right)^{+}\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\left({\operatorname{Ber}\left({p_{i}}\right)+W_{i}-r-1}\right)^{+}\right].

∑z≥0Pr[Wi=z](𝔼[(Poi(pi)+z−r−1)+−(Ber(pi)+z−r−1)+]).\sum_{z\geq 0}\Pr[W_{i}=z]\left({\mathbb{E}\left[\left({\operatorname{Poi}\left({p_{i}}\right)+z-r-1}\right)^{+}-\left({\operatorname{Ber}\left({p_{i}}\right)+z-r-1}\right)^{+}\right]}\right).

𝔼⁡[(Ber⁡(pi)+z−r−1)+]=0≤𝔼⁡[(Poi⁡(pi)+z−r−1)+].\mathbb{E}\left[\left({\operatorname{Ber}\left({p_{i}}\right)+z-r-1}\right)^{+}\right]=0\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\left({\operatorname{Poi}\left({p_{i}}\right)+z-r-1}\right)^{+}\right].

𝔼⁡[(Poi⁡(pi)+z−r−1)−(Ber⁡(pi)+z−r−1)]=𝔼⁡[Poi⁡(pi)]−𝔼⁡[Ber⁡(pi)]=0,\mathbb{E}\left[\left({\operatorname{Poi}\left({p_{i}}\right)+z-r-1}\right)-\left({\operatorname{Ber}\left({p_{i}}\right)+z-r-1}\right)\right]=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Poi}\left({p_{i}}\right)]-\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Ber}\left({p_{i}}\right)]=0,

since the two random variables have the same mean. Thus,

Dr=𝔼⁡[(X−r−1)+]−𝔼⁡[(Y−r−1)+]=𝔼⁡[(Vn−r−1)+]−𝔼⁡[(V0−r−1)+]≥0.D_{r}=\mathbb{E}[(X-r-1)^{+}]-\mathbb{E}[(Y-r-1)^{+}]=\mathbb{E}[(V_{n}-r-1)^{+}]-\mathbb{E}[(V_{0}-r-1)^{+}]\geq 0.

Therefore, applying Theorem B.3 to X,YX,Y yields Theorem B.1.

B.2 The Main Proof

We use the notation of Section 2 and assume ∑i=1npi=k\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=k. Recall the random-order acceptance-rate function from Section 4.1 (see also [5]): for t≥0t\geq 0,

ARk⁡(t)=min⁡{1,kt+1}.\operatorname{AR}_{k}(t)=\min\left\{1,\frac{k}{t+1}\right\}.

Also, let

γk=1−e−k​kkk!,δk=𝔼⁡[ARk⁡(Poi⁡(k−1))],αk=γkδk,βk=1−αk.\gamma_{k}=1-e^{-k}\frac{k^{k}}{k!},\qquad\delta_{k}=\mathbb{E}\left[\operatorname{AR}_{k}(\operatorname{Poi}\left({k-1}\right))\right],\qquad\alpha_{k}=\frac{\gamma_{k}}{\delta_{k}},\qquad\beta_{k}=1-\alpha_{k}.

Consider the following generalization of Algorithm 1 for general k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. When we observe an element ii that is both online-active and sample-active and we still have capacity to accept it, we accept it with probability αk\alpha_{k}. Let σ\sigma be the uniformly random arrival permutation, so that σ⁡(t)\sigma(t) is the element arriving in position tt. The set 𝒜\mathcal{A} contains the accepted elements, and StS_{t} is the number of elements accepted after the first tt arrivals.

For k=1k=1, we have δ1=1\delta_{1}=1 and thus

α1=γ1=1−1e,\alpha_{1}=\gamma_{1}=1-\frac{1}{e},

so the algorithm agrees with Algorithm 1 for the k=1k=1 case.

For each element ii, let ρi≔pi​(1−βk​pi)\rho_{i}\coloneqq p_{i}(1-\beta_{k}p_{i}), ξi∼Ber⁡(αk)\xi_{i}\sim\operatorname{Ber}\left({\alpha_{k}}\right), and

Zi≔Xi​((1−Yi)+Yi​ξi),Z_{i}\coloneqq X_{i}\left({(1-Y_{i})+Y_{i}\xi_{i}}\right),

where the ξi\xi_{i}’s are independent across elements and independent of the samples, online activations, and arrival order. We call an element ii with Zi=1Z_{i}=1 a candidate. Thus, an element is a candidate if it is online-active and either sample-inactive or sample-active with a successful coin ξi\xi_{i}. All ZiZ_{i}’s are independent, and

Pr[Zi=1]=pi((1−pi)+piαk)=pi(1−βkpi)=ρi.\Pr[Z_{i}=1]=p_{i}\left({(1-p_{i})+p_{i}\alpha_{k}}\right)=p_{i}(1-\beta_{k}p_{i})=\rho_{i}.

The parameter qiq_{i} in Algorithm 6 is the coin bias chosen after observing XiX_{i}, YiY_{i}, and the available capacity; ρi\rho_{i} is the unconditional probability that ii is a candidate. Recall that RiR_{i} is the event that the algorithm reaches ii. If i=σ⁡(t)i=\sigma(t), then Ri={St−1<k}R_{i}=\left\{S_{t-1}<k\right\}. Coupling ξi\xi_{i} with the algorithm’s coin whenever ii is online-active and sample-active gives Qi=𝟏Ri​ZiQ_{i}=\mathbf{1}_{R_{i}}Z_{i}. Hence Ai=Ri∩{Zi=1}A_{i}=R_{i}\cap\left\{Z_{i}=1\right\}, or equivalently, the algorithm scans the random order and accepts the first kk candidates.

Fix an element ii with pi>0p_{i}>0. Its conditional probability of being a candidate is

Pr⁡[Zi=1|Xi=1]=(1−pi)+pi​αk=1−βk​pi.\Pr\left[Z_{i}=1\>\middle|\>X_{i}=1\right]=(1-p_{i})+p_{i}\alpha_{k}=1-\beta_{k}p_{i}.

Also, let Gi=∑j≠iZjG_{i}=\sum_{j\neq i}Z_{j} denote the (random) number of elements that ii has to compete with for a spot, and notice that GiG_{i} is a sum of independent Bernoulli variables, each with parameter ρj\rho_{j}, and all independent of XiX_{i} and ZiZ_{i}. In other words, Gi∼PB⁡(ρ1,…,ρi−1,ρi+1,…,ρn)G_{i}\sim\operatorname{PB}\left({\rho_{1},\dots,\rho_{i-1},\rho_{i+1},\dots,\rho_{n}}\right). If Zi=1Z_{i}=1 and Gi=tG_{i}=t, then there are exactly t+1t+1 candidate elements including ii. Since the arrival order is uniformly random, ii is uniformly ranked among those t+1t+1 candidates. The event AiA_{i} occurs exactly when ii’s rank among candidates is at most kk. Thus,

Pr[Ai|Xi=1,Zi=1,Gi=t]=min{1,kt+1}=ARk(t).\Pr\left[A_{i}\>\middle|\>X_{i}=1,Z_{i}=1,G_{i}=t\right]=\min\left\{1,\frac{k}{t+1}\right\}=\operatorname{AR}_{k}(t).

Therefore, its conditional acceptance probability is

Ci=(1−βk​pi)⋅𝔼⁡[ARk⁡(Gi)].C_{i}=(1-\beta_{k}p_{i})\cdot\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{AR}_{k}(G_{i})]. (28)

To show that this is at least γk\gamma_{k} for all k≥1k\geq 1, we will make use of two lemmas. The first is a corollary of Theorem B.2 and its proof can be found in Section B.2.1.

Lemma B.1.

For every i∈[n]i\in[n], we have 𝔼⁡[ARk⁡(Gi)]≥𝔼⁡[ARk⁡(Poi⁡(k−pi))]\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{AR}_{k}(G_{i})]\geq\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{AR}_{k}(\operatorname{Poi}\left({k-p_{i}}\right))].

Notice that we cannot obtain the inequality in Lemma B.1 from Theorem B.1 in a black-box way, since ARk⁡(⋅)\operatorname{AR}_{k}(\cdot) is neither convex nor concave. Therefore, we develop a slightly more involved argument to prove the lemma.

The second lemma states that the reciprocal of 𝔼⁡[ARk⁡(Poi⁡(k−u))]\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{AR}_{k}(\operatorname{Poi}\left({k-u}\right))] is convex for u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1] and its proof can be found in Section B.2.2.

Lemma B.2.

For k≥2k\geq 2, let

Fk​(λ)=1𝔼⁡[ARk⁡(Poi⁡(λ))].F_{k}(\lambda)=\frac{1}{\mathbb{E}\left[\operatorname{AR}_{k}(\operatorname{Poi}\left({\lambda}\right))\right]}.

Then, Fk​(λ)F_{k}(\lambda) is convex in [k−1,k][k-1,k] or, in other words, Fk​(k−u)F_{k}(k-u) is convex for u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1].

We are finally ready to show that the Conservative Scaling algorithm is γk\gamma_{k}-balanced for every k≥1k\geq 1.

Theorem B.4.

The Conservative Scaling algorithm is γk\gamma_{k}-balanced for all k≥1k\geq 1.

Proof.

The case k=1k=1 follows from Section 3.1. Let k≥2k\geq 2. Fix an element ii with pi>0p_{i}>0. Combining Lemma B.1 with (28), we get

Ci≥(1−βk​pi)​𝔼​[ARk⁡(Poi⁡(k−pi))].C_{i}\geq(1-\beta_{k}p_{i})\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{AR}_{k}(\operatorname{Poi}\left({k-p_{i}}\right))]. (29)

Note that 1−βk​pi1-\beta_{k}p_{i} is the linear interpolation between 11 at pi=0p_{i}=0 and αk\alpha_{k} at pi=1p_{i}=1. Since, by Lemma B.2, the function Fk​(λ)=1/𝔼⁡[ARk⁡(Poi⁡(λ))]F_{k}(\lambda)=1/\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{AR}_{k}(\operatorname{Poi}\left({\lambda}\right))] is convex in [k−1,k][k-1,k], we have

Fk​(k−pi)≤(1−pi)​Fk​(k)+pi​Fk​(k−1).F_{k}(k-p_{i})\leq(1-p_{i})F_{k}(k)+p_{i}F_{k}(k-1).

Using the fact that Fk​(k)=1/γkF_{k}(k)=1/\gamma_{k} and Fk​(k−1)=1/δk=αk/γkF_{k}(k-1)=1/\delta_{k}=\alpha_{k}/\gamma_{k}, we have

Fk​(k−pi)≤1−piγk+αk​piγk=1−βk​piγk,F_{k}(k-p_{i})\leq\frac{1-p_{i}}{\gamma_{k}}+\frac{\alpha_{k}p_{i}}{\gamma_{k}}=\frac{1-\beta_{k}p_{i}}{\gamma_{k}},

which implies that

(1−βk​pi)​𝔼​[ARk⁡(Poi⁡(k−pi))]≥γk.∎(1-\beta_{k}p_{i})\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{AR}_{k}(\operatorname{Poi}\left({k-p_{i}}\right))]\geq\gamma_{k}.\qed

=∑r=0k−2(k−1)​λrr!+λk−1(k−2)!−∑r=1k−1r​λrr!\displaystyle=\sum_{r=0}^{k-2}\left({k-1}\right)\frac{\lambda^{r}}{r!}+\frac{\lambda^{k-1}}{(k-2)!}-\sum_{r=1}^{k-1}r\frac{\lambda^{r}}{r!}

=∑r=0k−2(k−1−r)​λrr!≥0.\displaystyle=\sum_{r=0}^{k-2}\left({k-1-r}\right)\frac{\lambda^{r}}{r!}\geq 0.

Putting everything together, we get that

Ψk​(λ)≥λ​1λk+1−λ+(λ−k+1)=(k+1−λ)+(λ−k+1)=2,\Psi_{k}(\lambda)\geq\lambda\frac{1}{\frac{\lambda}{k+1-\lambda}}+(\lambda-k+1)=(k+1-\lambda)+(\lambda-k+1)=2,

and the claim follows. ∎

Appendix C Monotonicity

In this section, we prove that all our schemes are monotone. At the end of this appendix we show how the balance guarantees can be extended to the case ∑ipi≤k\sum_{i}p_{i}\leq k. First, we show that, for every fixed p∈𝒫kp\in\mathcal{P}_{k} and every i∈A1⊆A2⊆[n]i\in A_{1}\subseteq A_{2}\subseteq[n],

Pr[i∈πp(A1)]≥Pr[i∈πp(A2)],\Pr\left[i\in\pi_{p}(A_{1})\right]\geq\Pr\left[i\in\pi_{p}(A_{2})\right], (40)

where the probabilities are over the samples, the internal randomness of the scheme, and, for an ROCRS, the uniformly random arrival order. The same arguments establish monotonicity for the offline CRSs obtained by running our ROCRSs in an independently generated uniformly random order.

We show (40) for each scheme in its own subsection; the extension of the balance guarantees is given at the end of this appendix.

C.1 The Conservative Scaling ROCRS

We start with the ROCRS of Section 3.1.

Proposition C.1.

Algorithm 1 is a monotone ROCRS.

Proof.

For each element jj, draw an independent coin ξj∼Ber⁡(1−1/e)\xi_{j}\sim\operatorname{Ber}\left({1-1/e}\right), independently of the samples, online activations, and arrival order, which plays the role of qjq_{j} in the algorithm. Let

H≔{j∈[n]|Yj=0​ or ​ξj=1}.H\coloneqq\left\{j\in[n]\>\middle|\>Y_{j}=0\text{ or }\xi_{j}=1\right\}.

On online-active set WW, the algorithm accepts the first element of W∩HW\cap H, if this set is non-empty. Condition on the samples, the coins, and the arrival order, and consider i∈A1⊆A2i\in A_{1}\subseteq A_{2}. If the algorithm accepts ii on W=A2W=A_{2}, then i∈Hi\in H and no element of A2∩HA_{2}\cap H precedes ii. Since A1∩H⊆A2∩HA_{1}\cap H\subseteq A_{2}\cap H, the same is true on W=A1W=A_{1}. By unconditioning, we obtain (40). ∎

Next, consider the Conservative Scaling ROCRS for general kk, found in Appendix B, which directly generalizes the k=1k=1 variant. Its parameter αk\alpha_{k} depends only on the capacity kk and thus the same argument as above with ξj∼Ber⁡(αk)\xi_{j}\sim\operatorname{Ber}\left({\alpha_{k}}\right) yields the following.

Proposition C.2.

Algorithm 6 is a monotone ROCRS.

Proposition C.4.

C.3 The Almost-Greedy ROCRS for General kk

Clearly, the simple ROCRS from Section 5.1 that greedily accepts the first kk online-active elements without using any samples is monotone. For the Almost-Greedy ROCRS, we compare acceptance probabilities by averaging over the samples, the coins, and the arrival order, using the rank calculation from Section 4.1.

Proposition C.6.

Algorithm 4 is a monotone ROCRS.

Proof.

Fix i∈A1⊆A2i\in A_{1}\subseteq A_{2}, and let μ=∑j=1npj≤k\mu=\sum_{j=1}^{n}p_{j}\leq k. If A1=A2A_{1}=A_{2}, then (40) trivially holds with equality, so assume that A1⊊A2A_{1}\subsetneq A_{2}. If |A1|≤k−1|A_{1}|\leq k-1, the algorithm accepts ii with probability one when W=A1W=A_{1}, which proves (40). Henceforth, assume that |A1|≥k|A_{1}|\geq k, so |A2|≥k+1|A_{2}|\geq k+1.

For either W=A1W=A_{1} or W=A2W=A_{2} with |W|≥k+1|W|\geq k+1, the relative arrival order of the elements of WW is uniformly random. Thus, each possible rank of ii has probability 1/|W|1/|W|. The first k−1k-1 ranks always lead to acceptance, contributing (k−1)/|W|(k-1)/|W| to the acceptance probability. If ii has rank kk, it is rejected exactly when its sample is active and its acceptance coin fails. These events are independent of each other and of the arrival order, so their joint probability is pi⋅k/(2​k+1)p_{i}\cdot k/(2k+1).

If ii has rank k+1k+1, it is accepted exactly when the element of rank kk is rejected. Conditional on ii having rank k+1k+1, each j∈W−ij\in W-i is equally likely to have rank kk, and that element is rejected with probability k​pj/(2​k+1)kp_{j}/(2k+1). Hence, the conditional acceptance probability at rank k+1k+1 is the average of these rejection probabilities over W−iW-i. At any later rank, the algorithm has already accepted kk elements and rejects ii. Adding the contributions, we obtain

Pr[i∈πp(W)]\displaystyle\Pr\left[i\in\pi_{p}(W)\right] =k−1|W|+1|W|​(1−k​pi2​k+1)+1|W|​(|W|−1)​∑j∈W−ik​pj2​k+1\displaystyle=\frac{k-1}{|W|}+\frac{1}{|W|}\left({1-\frac{kp_{i}}{2k+1}}\right)+\frac{1}{|W|(|W|-1)}\sum_{j\in W-i}\frac{kp_{j}}{2k+1}
=k|W|​(1−pi2​k+1+∑j∈W−ipj(2​k+1)​(|W|−1)).\displaystyle=\frac{k}{|W|}\left({1-\frac{p_{i}}{2k+1}+\frac{\sum_{j\in W-i}p_{j}}{(2k+1)(|W|-1)}}\right). (41)

If |A1|=k|A_{1}|=k, then ii is rejected on W=A1W=A_{1} only when it has rank kk and its sample and coin cause rejection. The probability of this event is (1/k)⋅pi⋅k/(2​k+1)=pi/(2​k+1)(1/k)\cdot p_{i}\cdot k/(2k+1)=p_{i}/(2k+1), so its acceptance probability is 1−pi/(2​k+1)1-p_{i}/(2k+1). To bound the acceptance probability on W=A2W=A_{2}, we use pi≥0p_{i}\geq 0 and ∑j∈A2−ipj≤|A2|−1\sum_{j\in A_{2}-i}p_{j}\leq|A_{2}|-1 in (41). This yields

Pr[i∈πp(A2)]\displaystyle\Pr\left[i\in\pi_{p}(A_{2})\right] ≤k|A2|​(1+12​k+1)≤kk+1​(1+12​k+1)=1−12​k+1≤1−pi2​k+1\displaystyle\leq\frac{k}{|A_{2}|}\left({1+\frac{1}{2k+1}}\right)\leq\frac{k}{k+1}\left({1+\frac{1}{2k+1}}\right)=1-\frac{1}{2k+1}\leq 1-\frac{p_{i}}{2k+1}

Finally, suppose that |A1|≥k+1|A_{1}|\geq k+1. For both W=A1W=A_{1} and W=A2W=A_{2}, partitioning the ground set into {i}\left\{i\right\}, W−iW-i, and the elements outside WW gives

μ=pi+∑j∈W−ipj+∑j∉Wpj.\mu=p_{i}+\sum_{j\in W-i}p_{j}+\sum_{j\notin W}p_{j}.

Factoring out k/(2​k+1)k/(2k+1) from (41), substituting the above identity for pip_{i} and combining the two coefficients of ∑j∈W−ipj\sum_{j\in W-i}p_{j}, using

1|W|+1|W|​(|W|−1)=1|W|−1,\frac{1}{|W|}+\frac{1}{|W|(|W|-1)}=\frac{1}{|W|-1},

yields

Pr[i∈πp(W)]\displaystyle\Pr\left[i\in\pi_{p}(W)\right] =k2​k+1​(2​k+1−pi|W|+∑j∈W−ipj|W|​(|W|−1))\displaystyle=\frac{k}{2k+1}\left({\frac{2k+1-p_{i}}{|W|}+\frac{\sum_{j\in W-i}p_{j}}{|W|(|W|-1)}}\right)

≥k2​k+1​(2​k+1−μ+∑j∉A2pj|A2|+∑j∈A2∖A1pj|A2|−1+∑j∈A1−ipj|A2|−1)\displaystyle\geq\frac{k}{2k+1}\left({\frac{2k+1-\mu+\sum_{j\notin A_{2}}p_{j}}{|A_{2}|}+\frac{\sum_{j\in A_{2}\setminus A_{1}}p_{j}}{|A_{2}|-1}+\frac{\sum_{j\in A_{1}-i}p_{j}}{|A_{2}|-1}}\right)
=Pr[i∈πp(A2)],\displaystyle=\Pr\left[i\in\pi_{p}(A_{2})\right],

where the inequality follows from the facts that |A1|≤|A2|−1|A_{1}|\leq|A_{2}|-1 and 2​k+1−μ≥k+12k+1-\mu\geq k+1. Thus, (40) holds in every case. ∎

Finally, consider the Count Test OCRS from Section 4.2. We use the equivalent description of the algorithm, found in the proof of Theorem 4.2, in which the algorithm chooses candidate positions uniformly at random.

Proposition C.7.

Algorithm 5 is a monotone OCRS for every fixed parameter rr.

Proof.

Fix RR and all samples, and let N=R+∑j=1nYjN=R+\sum_{j=1}^{n}Y_{j}. For an online-active set WW, let Bt​(W)B_{t}(W) be the difference between R+∑j=1tYjR+\sum_{j=1}^{t}Y_{j} and the number of candidates among the first tt elements. The same recursion as in the proof of Theorem 4.2 gives

Bt​(A1)≥Bt​(A2)for every ​t∈{0,…,n}.B_{t}(A_{1})\geq B_{t}(A_{2})\qquad\text{for every }t\in\left\{0,\dots,n\right\}.

Bt(A1)=(Bt−1(A1)+Yt−𝟏{t∈A1})+≥(Bt−1(A2)+Yt−𝟏{t∈A2})+=Bt(A2),B_{t}(A_{1})=\left({B_{t-1}(A_{1})+Y_{t}-\mathbf{1}_{\left\{t\in A_{1}\right\}}}\right)^{+}\geq\left({B_{t-1}(A_{2})+Y_{t}-\mathbf{1}_{\left\{t\in A_{2}\right\}}}\right)^{+}=B_{t}(A_{2}),

Bi−1​(A1)+Yi≥Bi−1​(A2)+Yi≥1,B_{i-1}(A_{1})+Y_{i}\geq B_{i-1}(A_{2})+Y_{i}\geq 1,

Pr[i∈πp(A1)|R,Y1,…,Yn]\displaystyle\Pr\left[i\in\pi_{p}(A_{1})\>\middle|\>R,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n}\right] =aN𝟏{Bi−1(A1)+Yi≥1}\displaystyle=a_{N}\mathbf{1}_{\left\{B_{i-1}(A_{1})+Y_{i}\geq 1\right\}}
≥aN𝟏{Bi−1(A2)+Yi≥1}=Pr[i∈πp(A2)|R,Y1,…,Yn],\displaystyle\geq a_{N}\mathbf{1}_{\left\{B_{i-1}(A_{2})+Y_{i}\geq 1\right\}}=\Pr\left[i\in\pi_{p}(A_{2})\>\middle|\>R,Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n}\right],

where the inequality follows from the fact that the factor aNa_{N} is the same for A1A_{1} and A2A_{2}, since NN does not depend on A1,A2A_{1},A_{2}. By unconditioning, we obtain (40). ∎

C.5 Extension

Random order.

For each of the two Conservative Scaling schemes, Almost-Greedy, and the zero-sample greedy scheme, append independent dummy elements whose probabilities sum to k−∑ipik-\sum_{i}p_{i}, splitting this mass among several elements if necessary. Keep the probabilities and samples of the original elements unchanged. In the resulting instance, forcing all dummy elements to be online-inactive leaves the distribution of every original acceptance decision unchanged, since the samples of inactive elements are never used, and the relative order of the original elements is still uniform. For the fixed resulting probability vector, the monotonicity of the active-set shows that allowing the dummy elements to be online-active can only decrease an original element’s acceptance probability. The guarantee for total mass kk therefore implies the same guarantee for the original instance.

The two-sample single-item OCRS.

Let μ=∑ipi≤1\mu=\sum_{i}p_{i}\leq 1 and recall that 𝒮={j:Yj(1)=1}\mathcal{S}=\{j:Y_{j}^{(1)}=1\}. Repeating the calculation in Appendix A.4, with 1−pi=(1−μ)+∑j≠ipj1-p_{i}=(1-\mu)+\sum_{j\neq i}p_{j}, gives

Pr[T=i]=pi2(1+(1−μ)𝔼[1|𝒮−i|+1]).\Pr[T=i]=\frac{p_{i}}{2}\left(1+(1-\mu)\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}-i|+1}\right]\right).

Indeed, conditional on Yi(1)=1Y_{i}^{(1)}=1, the singleton branch has probability 1−pi/21-p_{i}/2 of choosing ii, and the other branch contributes, on each set SS containing ii,

12​(1−μ|S|+∑j≠ipj|S−i−j|+1).\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1-\mu}{|S|}+\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{p_{j}}{|S-i-j|+1}\right).

Averaging and using ∑j≠ipj𝔼[1/(|𝒮−i−j|+1)]=Pr[𝒮−i≠∅]\sum_{j\neq i}p_{j}\mathbb{E}[1/(|\mathcal{S}-i-j|+1)]=\Pr[\mathcal{S}-i\neq\emptyset] proves the formula. Also,

∑ipi𝔼[1|𝒮−i|+1]=Pr[𝒮≠∅],Pr[T=0]=12+1−μ2Pr[𝒮=∅].\sum_{i}p_{i}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}-i|+1}\right]=\Pr[\mathcal{S}\neq\emptyset],\qquad\Pr[T=0]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1-\mu}{2}\Pr[\mathcal{S}=\emptyset].

Consequently Pr[T=0]≥1/2\Pr[T=0]\geq 1/2 and Pr[T=i]≥pi/2\Pr[T=i]\geq p_{i}/2 for every ii. Substitution in the non-negative sum in the proof of Lemma 3.1 yields Ci≥1/2C_{i}\geq 1/2.

The one-sample single-item OCRS.

Again write μ=∑ipi≤1\mu=\sum_{i}p_{i}\leq 1. The proof of Lemma 3.2 works with qi=∑j≠ipj≤1−piq_{i}=\sum_{j\neq i}p_{j}\leq 1-p_{i} and gives

εi≤pi​qi​(1−e−qi)12≤1−1/e12​pi​(1−pi).\varepsilon_{i}\leq\frac{p_{i}q_{i}(1-e^{-q_{i}})}{12}\leq\frac{1-1/e}{12}p_{i}(1-p_{i}).

Use the ideal threshold with Pr[T∗=0]=1−μ/2\Pr[T^{*}=0]=1-\mu/2 and Pr[T∗=i]=pi/2\Pr[T^{*}=i]=p_{i}/2. The same telescoping identity gives

𝔼⁡[gℓ​(T∗)]=12+1−μ2​gℓ​(0)≥12.\mathbb{E}[g_{\ell}(T^{*})]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1-\mu}{2}g_{\ell}(0)\geq\frac{1}{2}.

The actual threshold moves εi\varepsilon_{i} mass from each ii to 00. The same loss calculation as in Theorem 3.4, followed by Lemma 3.3, therefore gives

Cℓ≥12−∑i<ℓεi​(gℓ​(i)−gℓ​(0))≥12−1−1/e32>0.48.C_{\ell}\geq\frac{1}{2}-\sum_{i<\ell}\varepsilon_{i}\bigl(g_{\ell}(i)-g_{\ell}(0)\bigr)\geq\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1-1/e}{32}>0.48.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
